lectures.title: Day 5: Vulnerabilities and Indicators of Malicious Activity
lectures.content:
# Day 5 — Vulnerabilities and Indicators of Malicious Activity

## Module 2: Threats, Vulnerabilities & Mitigations | Session 5 of 14

| | |
|:---|:---|
| **Duration** | 2 hours (120 minutes) |
| **Exam Domain** | 2.0 — Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Mitigations (22%) |
| **Objectives Covered** | 2.3, 2.4 |
| **Delivery** | Live online (Zoom/Teams), bilingual English/Arabic |

---

## Session Overview

This session is one of the most technically dense in the entire course, covering the full taxonomy of vulnerabilities and the indicators that reveal when those vulnerabilities have been exploited. Objective 2.3 catalogs vulnerabilities across applications, operating systems, web platforms, hardware, virtualization, cloud environments, supply chains, and mobile devices. Students must understand not just what each vulnerability is, but how it is exploited and why it exists — the exam frequently presents scenarios where students must identify the vulnerability type from a description of an attack.

Objective 2.4 shifts from vulnerabilities to active threats — the indicators of malicious activity that security professionals must recognize. This includes the complete malware taxonomy (ransomware, trojans, worms, spyware, keyloggers, rootkits, and more), physical attacks, network attacks (DDoS, DNS attacks, on-path attacks), application attacks (injection, privilege escalation, directory traversal), cryptographic attacks, and password attacks. Critically, students will also learn the behavioral indicators that suggest an attack is underway: account lockouts, impossible travel, resource consumption anomalies, and missing logs.

The volume of material in this session is substantial. The instructor should prioritize depth on the most heavily tested topics — malware types, web vulnerabilities (SQLi, XSS), and network attacks (DDoS) — while ensuring all topics receive adequate coverage.

---

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this session, students will be able to:

1. **Classify** vulnerabilities by category: application, OS-based, web-based, hardware, virtualization, cloud-specific, supply chain, mobile, and cryptographic.
2. **Explain** specific vulnerability types including buffer overflow, race conditions, SQL injection, XSS, VM escape, and zero-day.
3. **Identify** all nine malware types tested on the SY0-701 exam and describe how each operates.
4. **Differentiate** between network attack types: DDoS (amplified, reflected), DNS attacks, on-path attacks, and credential replay.
5. **Recognize** indicators of malicious activity including account lockout, impossible travel, resource consumption anomalies, and missing logs.
6. **Analyze** a scenario to determine the type of attack and the vulnerability being exploited.

---

## Exam Objectives Covered

| Objective | Description |
|:---|:---|
| **2.3** | Explain various types of vulnerabilities |
| **2.4** | Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity |

---

## Detailed Session Outline

| Time Block | Duration | Topic | Activity Type | Details |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 0:00–0:05 | 5 min | **Recap & Session Preview** | Lecture | Quick review of Day 4 (threat actors, vectors). Preview today's two objectives. |
| 0:05–0:20 | 15 min | **Application Vulnerabilities** | Lecture | Cover: **Memory injection** (injecting code into a running process's memory space), **Buffer overflow** (writing data beyond allocated memory — can allow code execution), **Race conditions** — **Time-of-check (TOC)** and **Time-of-use (TOU)** (exploiting the gap between checking a condition and acting on it), **Malicious update** (compromised software updates). Explain each with a simple diagram or analogy. |
| 0:20–0:30 | 10 min | **Web-Based and OS Vulnerabilities** | Lecture | Cover: **SQL injection (SQLi)** (inserting malicious SQL into input fields to manipulate databases — demonstrate with a simple example: `' OR 1=1 --`), **Cross-site scripting (XSS)** (injecting malicious scripts into web pages viewed by other users — stored vs. reflected). **OS-based vulnerabilities** (unpatched operating systems, privilege escalation through OS flaws). |
| 0:30–0:40 | 10 min | **Hardware, Virtualization, Cloud, and Supply Chain Vulnerabilities** | Lecture | Cover: **Hardware** — Firmware vulnerabilities, End-of-life hardware (no more updates), Legacy systems. **Virtualization** — VM escape (breaking out of a virtual machine to access the hypervisor or other VMs), Resource reuse (data remnants in shared resources). **Cloud-specific** (misconfigured storage buckets, shared responsibility model failures). **Supply chain** — Service/hardware/software provider compromises. **Cryptographic** vulnerabilities (weak algorithms, short key lengths). |
| 0:40–0:50 | 10 min | **Mobile and Misconfiguration Vulnerabilities** | Lecture | Cover: **Misconfiguration** (the most common vulnerability — default settings, open permissions, unnecessary services). **Mobile device** — Side loading (installing apps from outside official app stores), Jailbreaking (removing manufacturer restrictions — exposes device to unsigned code). **Zero-day** (a vulnerability unknown to the vendor with no available patch — the most dangerous category). |
| 0:50–0:55 | 5 min | **Break** | — | — |
| 0:55–1:15 | 20 min | **Malware Types** | Lecture + Visuals | Systematic coverage of all nine types: **Ransomware** (encrypts data, demands payment), **Trojan** (disguised as legitimate software), **Worm** (self-replicating, spreads without user action), **Spyware** (monitors user activity), **Bloatware** (unwanted pre-installed software — not always malicious but consumes resources), **Virus** (requires host file, activated by user action), **Keylogger** (records keystrokes), **Logic bomb** (malicious code triggered by a specific condition — date, event, user action), **Rootkit** (hides deep in the OS, extremely difficult to detect — often modifies the kernel). Use a comparison table. |
| 1:15–1:25 | 10 min | **Physical and Network Attacks** | Lecture | **Physical attacks**: Brute force (physical — forcing entry), RFID cloning (copying access badge data), Environmental (power, temperature, water damage). **Network attacks**: **DDoS** — Amplified (attacker sends small request, server responds with large reply to victim), Reflected (attacker spoofs victim's IP, third-party servers send responses to victim); **DNS attacks** (DNS poisoning, DNS hijacking); **Wireless attacks** (evil twin, rogue AP); **On-path attack** (attacker intercepts communication between two parties — formerly man-in-the-middle); **Credential replay** (capturing and reusing authentication credentials); **Malicious code** injection into network traffic. |
| 1:25–1:35 | 10 min | **Application, Cryptographic, and Password Attacks** | Lecture | **Application attacks**: Injection, Buffer overflow, Replay (resending captured legitimate requests), Privilege escalation (gaining higher access than authorized), Forgery (CSRF — tricking a user's browser into making unauthorized requests), Directory traversal (accessing files outside the intended directory using ../ paths). **Cryptographic attacks**: Downgrade (forcing use of weaker encryption), Collision (two inputs producing the same hash), Birthday (exploiting probability to find hash collisions). **Password attacks**: Spraying (trying one common password against many accounts), Brute force (trying all possible combinations). |
| 1:35–1:50 | 15 min | **Indicators of Malicious Activity** | Lecture | Cover all indicators: **Account lockout** (multiple failed login attempts), **Concurrent session usage** (same account logged in from multiple locations), **Blocked content** (security tools blocking unusual outbound traffic), **Impossible travel** (logins from geographically distant locations in an impossibly short time), **Resource consumption** (unusual CPU, memory, bandwidth, or disk usage), **Resource inaccessibility** (systems or services unexpectedly unavailable), **Out-of-cycle logging** (log entries at unusual times), **Published/documented** (indicators published by threat intelligence feeds), **Missing logs** (log entries deleted to cover tracks — a strong indicator of compromise). |
| 1:50–2:10 | 20 min | **Attack Identification Exercise** | Interactive Activity | Present 10 attack scenarios. Students identify: (a) the vulnerability exploited, (b) the type of attack, and (c) any indicators that would have been visible. Discuss each answer. |
| 2:10–2:20 | 10 min | **Session Summary & Preview** | Wrap-up | Recap vulnerabilities, malware, attacks, and indicators. Preview Day 6: Mitigation Techniques. |

---

## Key Concepts & Definitions

| Term | Definition |
|:---|:---|
| **Buffer Overflow** | A vulnerability where a program writes data beyond the boundaries of allocated memory, potentially allowing an attacker to execute arbitrary code. |
| **SQL Injection (SQLi)** | A web vulnerability where an attacker inserts malicious SQL statements into input fields, manipulating the backend database to extract, modify, or delete data. |
| **Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)** | A web vulnerability where an attacker injects malicious scripts into web pages that are then executed in other users' browsers. |
| **VM Escape** | An attack where a process running inside a virtual machine breaks out to interact with the host operating system or hypervisor. |
| **Zero-Day** | A vulnerability that is unknown to the software vendor and for which no patch exists. Extremely dangerous because there is no defense until discovered. |
| **Ransomware** | Malware that encrypts a victim's files and demands payment (typically cryptocurrency) for the decryption key. |
| **Rootkit** | Malware that embeds itself deep in the operating system (often at the kernel level), hiding its presence and the presence of other malware. |
| **Logic Bomb** | Malicious code embedded in a system that executes when a specific condition is met (e.g., a date, a user action, or the deletion of an account). |
| **DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service)** | An attack where multiple compromised systems flood a target with traffic, overwhelming its resources and making it unavailable. |
| **On-Path Attack** | An attack where the adversary positions themselves between two communicating parties, intercepting and potentially modifying traffic. Formerly called man-in-the-middle. |
| **Privilege Escalation** | An attack where a user gains higher access permissions than they are authorized to have, either vertically (user → admin) or horizontally (user A → user B). |
| **Impossible Travel** | A security indicator where a user account logs in from two geographically distant locations within a timeframe that makes physical travel impossible. |
| **Credential Replay** | An attack where captured authentication credentials or session tokens are reused to gain unauthorized access. |

---

## Real-World Examples & Scenarios

**Scenario 1 — SQL Injection on a Government Portal**
A government e-services portal in the MENA region allows citizens to check the status of applications by entering their national ID number. An attacker enters `' OR '1'='1' --` into the ID field, causing the database to return all records instead of just one. The attacker now has access to personal data for thousands of citizens. This is a classic SQL injection attack exploiting a web-based vulnerability caused by insufficient input validation.

**Scenario 2 — Ransomware Attack on a Hospital**
A hospital in Amman receives a phishing email with a malicious attachment disguised as a patient referral document. When opened, the attachment executes ransomware that encrypts the hospital's electronic health records and demands 5 Bitcoin for the decryption key. Indicators include sudden resource inaccessibility (staff cannot access patient records), unusual resource consumption (encryption process consuming CPU), and blocked content (the ransomware attempting to communicate with a command-and-control server).

**Scenario 3 — Impossible Travel Detection**
A security analyst at a UAE-based company notices that an employee's account logged in from Dubai at 9:00 AM and from Moscow at 9:15 AM. Since physical travel between these locations in 15 minutes is impossible, this is flagged as an impossible travel indicator. Investigation reveals the employee's credentials were compromised through a credential replay attack — the attacker captured the session token from an unsecured Wi-Fi network.

**Scenario 4 — Logic Bomb by a Departing Employee**
A systems administrator at a technology company in Saudi Arabia, upon learning they will be terminated, plants a logic bomb in a critical database script. The code is set to execute 30 days after the administrator's account is deactivated, deleting all customer records. The logic bomb is an insider threat leveraging a time-based trigger. Detection would require code review, change management controls, and monitoring of out-of-cycle system modifications.

---

## Instructor Notes

**Common Misconceptions:**
- Students confuse **viruses** and **worms**. A virus requires a host file and user action to spread; a worm is self-replicating and spreads autonomously across networks.
- **Trojan** is not a virus. A Trojan does not self-replicate — it relies on social engineering to trick the user into installing it.
- Students often think **DDoS** and **DoS** are the same. DoS comes from a single source; DDoS comes from multiple distributed sources (a botnet). The exam uses DDoS specifically.
- **On-path attack** is the current CompTIA term for what was previously called "man-in-the-middle" (MITM). Use the current terminology.
- **Bloatware** is included in the malware list but is not always malicious — it refers to unwanted pre-installed software that consumes resources. The exam may test whether students recognize it as a security concern.

**Exam Emphasis:**
- Malware identification is heavily tested. Students must be able to identify the malware type from a behavioral description.
- SQLi and XSS are the most commonly tested web vulnerabilities. Know the difference: SQLi targets the database; XSS targets the user's browser.
- Indicators of malicious activity questions present a scenario and ask "which indicator is being observed?" Know all nine indicators.
- Zero-day questions often test whether students understand that no patch exists — making detection and response (rather than prevention) the primary defense.

**Teaching Tips:**
- For buffer overflow, use the analogy of pouring water into a glass that is too small — the overflow goes somewhere unintended, and an attacker can control where.
- For SQLi, show the actual SQL statement being manipulated. Even non-programmers can understand `SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = '' OR '1'='1'`.
- For malware, build a comparison table with columns: Name, How it Spreads, What it Does, Key Characteristic.
- For indicators, emphasize that **missing logs** is one of the strongest indicators of compromise — attackers delete logs to cover their tracks.

---

## Discussion Questions

1. "A web application allows users to search for products by name. An attacker enters a script tag in the search field, and the script executes in other users' browsers. What vulnerability is this, and how could it have been prevented?"

2. "Your SIEM alerts you that a single user account has been locked out 47 times in the past hour. What type of attack might be underway, and what should your immediate response be?"

3. "An organization discovers that its cloud storage bucket containing customer data has been publicly accessible for six months. No one configured it to be public — it was the default setting. What type of vulnerability is this?"

4. "Why are rootkits considered one of the most dangerous types of malware? What makes them particularly difficult to detect and remove?"

---

## Hands-On Activity: Malware Identification Challenge

**Objective:** Students read 9 behavioral descriptions and identify the correct malware type.

| # | Behavioral Description | Malware Type |
|:---|:---|:---|
| 1 | All files on the accounting department's shared drive are suddenly encrypted. A text file on the desktop demands payment in cryptocurrency within 72 hours. | Ransomware |
| 2 | A user downloads what appears to be a free PDF reader. After installation, the application works normally, but in the background it opens a backdoor allowing remote access. | Trojan |
| 3 | A network administrator notices that a single infected workstation has spread malware to 200 other machines on the network without any user interaction. | Worm |
| 4 | An employee's computer is running slowly. Investigation reveals a hidden program sending screenshots and browsing history to an external server every 30 minutes. | Spyware |
| 5 | A new company laptop comes pre-installed with 15 applications the user did not request, consuming 40% of available disk space and slowing boot times. | Bloatware |
| 6 | A user opens an infected Word document. The malware attaches itself to other Word documents on the system but does not spread until those documents are shared. | Virus |
| 7 | A security investigation reveals that every keystroke typed on a compromised workstation — including passwords and credit card numbers — has been recorded in a hidden file. | Keylogger |
| 8 | Three months after a disgruntled developer was terminated, a script executes at midnight that drops all tables in the production database. | Logic Bomb |
| 9 | A forensic analyst discovers that the operating system's kernel has been modified to hide certain processes and files from all standard monitoring tools. | Rootkit |

---

## Session Summary

- **Vulnerabilities** span applications (buffer overflow, race conditions), web platforms (SQLi, XSS), hardware (firmware, end-of-life), virtualization (VM escape), cloud, supply chain, mobile (side loading, jailbreaking), and cryptographic weaknesses.
- **Zero-day vulnerabilities** are the most dangerous because no patch exists at the time of discovery.
- **Misconfiguration** is the single most common vulnerability — default settings, open permissions, and unnecessary services.
- **Nine malware types** are tested: ransomware, Trojan, worm, spyware, bloatware, virus, keylogger, logic bomb, and rootkit. Each has distinct behavior and propagation methods.
- **Network attacks** include DDoS (amplified/reflected), DNS attacks, on-path attacks, and credential replay.
- **Indicators of malicious activity** include account lockout, concurrent sessions, impossible travel, resource consumption anomalies, resource inaccessibility, out-of-cycle logging, and missing logs.
- On the exam, expect scenario-based questions requiring identification of the vulnerability, attack type, or indicator from a description.

---

## Preparation for Next Session

Day 6 covers **mitigation techniques** (objective 2.5) — the defenses that address the vulnerabilities and attacks covered today. Students will learn about segmentation, access control, patching, encryption, monitoring, least privilege, and hardening techniques. This session completes Module 2 and ends with the **Module 2 Quiz (25 questions)**. Students should review the vulnerabilities and attack types from today's session, as the quiz will draw heavily from Days 4–6.

lectures.title: Day 6: Mitigation Techniques and Enterprise Security
lectures.content:
# Day 6 — Mitigation Techniques and Enterprise Security

## Module 2: Threats, Vulnerabilities & Mitigations | Session 6 of 14

| | |
|:---|:---|
| **Duration** | 2 hours (120 minutes) |
| **Exam Domain** | 2.0 — Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Mitigations (22%) |
| **Objectives Covered** | 2.5 |
| **Delivery** | Live online (Zoom/Teams), bilingual English/Arabic |
| **Assessment** | Module 2 Quiz (25 questions) administered at end of session |

---

## Session Overview

After two sessions spent cataloging the threats, vulnerabilities, and attack techniques that organizations face, this session answers the critical question: what do we do about them? Objective 2.5 covers the mitigation techniques used to secure the enterprise — the defensive toolkit that security professionals deploy to reduce risk, limit damage, and harden systems against exploitation.

The material in this session is inherently practical. Segmentation, access control, patching, encryption, and monitoring are not abstract concepts — they are daily operational realities for IT security teams. Students will learn how each technique addresses specific vulnerabilities and attack types covered in Days 4 and 5, creating a direct connection between offense and defense. The hardening techniques section is particularly important for the exam, covering endpoint protection, host-based firewalls, HIPS, disabling unnecessary ports and protocols, changing default passwords, and removing unnecessary software.

This is the final session of Module 2. The last 20 minutes are reserved for the Module 2 Quiz (25 questions), which covers all material from Days 4–6 (objectives 2.1 through 2.5).

---

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this session, students will be able to:

1. **Explain** the purpose and implementation of network segmentation as a mitigation technique.
2. **Describe** access control mechanisms including ACLs and permission models.
3. **Evaluate** the role of patching, encryption, and monitoring in reducing organizational risk.
4. **Apply** the principle of least privilege to a given access control scenario.
5. **Identify** hardening techniques: endpoint protection, host-based firewalls, HIPS, disabling ports/protocols, default password changes, and software removal.
6. **Recommend** appropriate mitigation techniques for specific vulnerability and attack scenarios.

---

## Exam Objectives Covered

| Objective | Description |
|:---|:---|
| **2.5** | Explain the purpose of mitigation techniques used to secure the enterprise |

---

## Detailed Session Outline

| Time Block | Duration | Topic | Activity Type | Details |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 0:00–0:05 | 5 min | **Recap & Session Preview** | Lecture | Quick review of Days 4–5 (threats, vulnerabilities, indicators). Frame today's session: "Now we learn how to defend." |
| 0:05–0:15 | 10 min | **Segmentation** | Lecture + Diagram | Define network segmentation: dividing a network into isolated segments to limit lateral movement. Cover physical segmentation (separate hardware) vs. logical segmentation (VLANs, subnets). Explain how segmentation limits the blast radius of a breach. Example: separating the guest Wi-Fi from the corporate network, isolating IoT devices, creating a DMZ. |
| 0:15–0:25 | 10 min | **Access Control** | Lecture | Cover: **Access Control Lists (ACLs)** — rules that define which users or systems can access which resources. **Permissions** — read, write, execute, and how they are assigned. Tie back to the AAA framework from Day 1. Emphasize that access control is both a preventive and a detective control. |
| 0:25–0:35 | 10 min | **Application Allow List and Isolation** | Lecture | **Application allow list** (only approved applications can run — blocks unknown/unauthorized software; contrast with deny list approach). **Isolation** (separating compromised or high-risk systems from the rest of the network — used during incident response and for high-security environments). |
| 0:35–0:45 | 10 min | **Patching and Encryption** | Lecture | **Patching** — the single most effective mitigation for known vulnerabilities. Cover patch management lifecycle: identify, test, deploy, verify. Discuss challenges: legacy systems, compatibility, downtime. **Encryption** — protects data confidentiality at rest and in transit. Tie back to Day 3 cryptography concepts. Emphasize encryption as both a preventive control and a compliance requirement. |
| 0:45–0:55 | 10 min | **Monitoring, Least Privilege, and Configuration Enforcement** | Lecture | **Monitoring** — continuous observation of systems, networks, and user behavior to detect anomalies. Tie to indicators from Day 5. **Least privilege** — users and systems should have only the minimum access necessary to perform their functions. Examples: a developer should not have admin access to production databases; a receptionist should not have access to HR records. **Configuration enforcement** — ensuring systems maintain approved configurations through automated tools and policies. |
| 0:55–1:00 | 5 min | **Break** | — | — |
| 1:00–1:05 | 5 min | **Decommissioning** | Lecture | Properly retiring systems that are no longer needed. Cover: data sanitization (wiping data before disposal), physical destruction of storage media, certificate of destruction, removing decommissioned systems from network access and inventory. Tie to asset management (covered in Module 4). |
| 1:05–1:25 | 20 min | **Hardening Techniques** | Lecture + Checklist | Systematic coverage of all hardening techniques: **Encryption** (encrypt sensitive data at rest and in transit), **Installation of endpoint protection** (antivirus, anti-malware, EDR agents), **Host-based firewall** (software firewall on individual systems — Windows Firewall, iptables), **Host-based intrusion prevention system (HIPS)** (monitors and blocks suspicious activity on the host), **Disabling ports/protocols** (close unnecessary network ports, disable insecure protocols like Telnet, FTP), **Default password changes** (change all factory-set passwords immediately upon deployment), **Removal of unnecessary software** (reduce attack surface by uninstalling unused applications and services). Build a hardening checklist on screen. |
| 1:25–1:40 | 15 min | **Mitigation Mapping Exercise** | Interactive Activity | Present 8 attack/vulnerability scenarios from Days 4–5. Students identify the most appropriate mitigation technique(s) for each. Example: "An attacker exploits a known vulnerability in an unpatched web server" → Patching. "A worm spreads laterally across the entire flat network" → Segmentation. |
| 1:40–1:45 | 5 min | **Module 2 Summary** | Wrap-up | Recap the entire module: threat actors and motivations, attack vectors, vulnerabilities, indicators, and mitigation techniques. Transition to quiz. |
| 1:45–2:05 | 20 min | **Module 2 Quiz** | Assessment | 25 multiple-choice questions covering objectives 2.1–2.5. Timed at 20 minutes. |
| 2:05–2:20 | 15 min | **Quiz Review & Preview** | Review + Preview | Review quiz answers. Preview Module 3: Security Architecture (Days 7–9). |

---

## Key Concepts & Definitions

| Term | Definition |
|:---|:---|
| **Segmentation** | Dividing a network into separate segments or zones to limit lateral movement and contain breaches. |
| **Access Control List (ACL)** | A set of rules that specifies which users or systems are granted or denied access to a particular resource. |
| **Application Allow List** | A security approach where only pre-approved applications are permitted to execute on a system. All other applications are blocked by default. |
| **Isolation** | Separating a system or network segment from others to prevent the spread of threats or to protect sensitive resources. |
| **Patching** | The process of applying updates to software or firmware to fix known vulnerabilities and improve security. |
| **Least Privilege** | The principle that users, processes, and systems should be granted only the minimum level of access necessary to perform their functions. |
| **Configuration Enforcement** | The use of automated tools and policies to ensure that systems maintain approved security configurations and do not drift from baseline settings. |
| **Decommissioning** | The process of securely retiring a system, including data sanitization, removal from the network, and documentation. |
| **Endpoint Protection** | Security software installed on individual devices (endpoints) to detect, prevent, and respond to threats. Includes antivirus, anti-malware, and EDR. |
| **Host-Based Firewall** | A software firewall running on an individual system that controls inbound and outbound network traffic for that specific host. |
| **HIPS (Host-Based Intrusion Prevention System)** | Software that monitors activity on a single host and can block suspicious behavior in real time, such as unauthorized file modifications or process execution. |
| **Hardening** | The process of reducing a system's attack surface by removing unnecessary software, disabling unused services, applying patches, and enforcing secure configurations. |

---

## Real-World Examples & Scenarios

**Scenario 1 — Segmentation Prevents Lateral Movement**
A retail company in Dubai segments its network into three zones: point-of-sale (POS) systems, corporate workstations, and guest Wi-Fi. When an attacker compromises a guest Wi-Fi user's device, they cannot pivot to the POS network because the segments are isolated by firewall rules and VLANs. Without segmentation, the attacker could have moved laterally from the guest network to the POS systems and exfiltrated credit card data.

**Scenario 2 — Patching Prevents Exploitation**
A university in Jordan runs a web application on an Apache server with a known vulnerability (CVE published 3 months ago). The IT team has not applied the patch due to concerns about compatibility. An attacker scans the internet for vulnerable Apache servers, finds the university's server, and exploits the vulnerability to deface the website. The mitigation was straightforward: patch the server. The university's failure was a process failure — no patch management lifecycle was in place.

**Scenario 3 — Least Privilege Limits Damage**
An accounting firm implements least privilege by restricting each accountant's access to only their assigned client files. When one accountant's credentials are compromised through phishing, the attacker can only access that accountant's client data — not the entire firm's client database. Without least privilege, the attacker would have had access to all client records.

**Scenario 4 — Hardening a New Server**
A cloud infrastructure team in Saudi Arabia deploys a new Linux server. Their hardening checklist includes: change the default root password, disable SSH root login, close all ports except 443 (HTTPS) and 22 (SSH), install and configure the host-based firewall (iptables), install endpoint protection (CrowdStrike agent), remove unnecessary packages (FTP server, Telnet), and enable audit logging. Each step reduces the attack surface.

---

## Instructor Notes

**Common Misconceptions:**
- Students often think **patching** is a simple, risk-free process. Emphasize that patches must be tested before deployment — a patch can introduce new bugs or break compatibility. This is why change management (Day 3) matters.
- **Allow list** vs. **deny list**: students may confuse the two. Allow list = only approved items are permitted (whitelist). Deny list = everything is permitted except blocked items (blacklist). Allow list is more secure but more restrictive.
- Students may think **least privilege** only applies to user accounts. It also applies to service accounts, applications, and system processes.
- **Segmentation** is not just about VLANs. It includes physical segmentation, micro-segmentation (in cloud/SDN environments), and application-level segmentation.

**Exam Emphasis:**
- Mitigation technique questions are almost always scenario-based: "Which technique would best mitigate this risk?" Know the primary use case for each technique.
- **Hardening** is a broad topic — expect questions that test specific techniques (disabling ports, changing defaults, removing software).
- **Least privilege** and **segmentation** are the two most commonly tested mitigation concepts.
- Questions may present a scenario where multiple mitigations apply — students must choose the **most effective** or **most appropriate** one.

**Teaching Tips:**
- Build a "Threat → Vulnerability → Mitigation" mapping table on screen, connecting material from all three sessions in Module 2.
- For hardening, walk through a real server hardening checklist step by step. Students find this practical and memorable.
- Emphasize that mitigation is about **reducing risk**, not eliminating it. No system is 100% secure — the goal is to make attacks more difficult, more detectable, and less damaging.

---

## Discussion Questions

1. "Your organization has a flat network with no segmentation. A single compromised workstation has access to every server, printer, and IoT device. What is your segmentation strategy, and what are the first three segments you would create?"

2. "A legacy application critical to your business cannot be patched because the vendor no longer supports it. What compensating controls would you implement?"

3. "An employee argues that least privilege slows down their work because they constantly need to request access. How do you balance security with productivity?"

4. "Your organization's hardening standard requires disabling USB ports on all workstations. Some employees need USB access for legitimate work. How do you handle this?"

---

## Hands-On Activity: Mitigation Mapping

**Objective:** Students map specific attacks/vulnerabilities to the most appropriate mitigation technique(s).

| # | Attack / Vulnerability | Primary Mitigation | Secondary Mitigation |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 1 | A worm spreads across the entire network because all systems are on the same subnet. | Segmentation | Endpoint protection |
| 2 | An attacker exploits a known SQL injection vulnerability in a web application. | Patching (fix the code) | Application allow list / Input validation |
| 3 | A former employee's account is still active and is used to access sensitive files. | Decommissioning (deprovisioning) | Least privilege / Monitoring |
| 4 | An unauthorized application installed by a user introduces malware to the network. | Application allow list | Endpoint protection / Least privilege |
| 5 | An attacker gains access to a database server using the default administrator password. | Default password changes (hardening) | Access control / Monitoring |
| 6 | Sensitive customer data is stolen from a laptop that was left in a taxi. | Encryption (full-disk) | Access control |
| 7 | An attacker escalates privileges on a server by exploiting an unnecessary service running on port 21 (FTP). | Disabling ports/protocols (hardening) | Patching / Least privilege |
| 8 | A compromised IoT device on the corporate network is used as a pivot point to attack internal servers. | Segmentation / Isolation | Monitoring / Configuration enforcement |

---

## Session Summary

- **Segmentation** limits lateral movement by dividing the network into isolated zones — one of the most effective mitigations against worms and lateral attacks.
- **Access control** (ACLs and permissions) restricts who can access what, enforcing the principle of least privilege.
- **Application allow listing** permits only approved software to run, blocking unauthorized and potentially malicious applications.
- **Patching** is the most effective mitigation for known vulnerabilities but requires a structured patch management process.
- **Least privilege** ensures users and systems have only the minimum access necessary — limiting the damage from compromised accounts.
- **Hardening techniques** reduce the attack surface: endpoint protection, host-based firewalls, HIPS, disabling unnecessary ports/protocols, changing default passwords, and removing unnecessary software.
- **Decommissioning** ensures retired systems are properly sanitized and removed from the network.
- Mitigation is about **risk reduction**, not risk elimination. The goal is defense in depth — multiple layers of controls working together.

---

## Preparation for Next Session

Day 7 begins **Module 3: Security Architecture**, covering exam objective 3.1 — architecture models and infrastructure concepts. Students will explore cloud architectures (responsibility matrix, hybrid considerations), infrastructure as code, serverless computing, microservices, containerization, virtualization, IoT, ICS/SCADA, and the considerations that drive architecture decisions (availability, resilience, scalability, cost). This module shifts the focus from individual threats and controls to the broader architectural decisions that shape an organization's security posture.

quiz.title: Module 2: Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Mitigations Quiz
quiz.description: End-of-module quiz covering Module 2: Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Mitigations

questions.questionText: A junior network administrator recently configured a new server and, to save time, used a common administrative password found in an online forum. An external attacker, with no specific knowledge of the organization, successfully guessed the password and gained access. Which of the following BEST describes this threat actor?
questions.explanation: Unskilled attacker.** An unskilled attacker (or "script kiddie") often uses simple, well-known techniques and tools, such as guessing common passwords, without needing deep technical knowledge.

questions.questionText: A financial services company notices a significant and sustained increase in sophisticated network probes originating from a country with which it has no business dealings. The activity appears focused on identifying vulnerabilities in their core banking systems, but no data has been exfiltrated yet. Which threat actor is MOST likely responsible, given the high level of sophistication and targeted nature of the reconnaissance?
questions.explanation: Nation-state.** Nation-state actors possess significant resources, sophistication, and funding. Their motivations often include espionage and targeting critical infrastructure, which aligns with the scenario.

questions.questionText: An employee receives an email with a subject line "Urgent: Action Required for Your Payroll Account" that contains a link to a website that looks identical to the company's HR portal. The employee is prompted to enter their credentials to prevent their account from being suspended. This is an example of which type of attack vector?
questions.explanation: Message-based (Phishing).** Phishing attacks use deceptive emails, texts, or other messages to trick recipients into revealing sensitive information or deploying malware.

questions.questionText: A security analyst discovers that a popular open-source library used in the company's main web application has a newly disclosed vulnerability that allows for remote code execution. The company has not yet applied the patch. This represents what kind of vulnerability?
questions.explanation: Zero-day vulnerability.** A zero-day is a vulnerability that has been disclosed but is not yet patched. The company's failure to apply the patch leaves them open to exploitation.

questions.questionText: During a security audit, a consultant finds that several servers in the datacenter are running an operating system that the vendor stopped supporting over a year ago. No security patches have been released since the end-of-life date. This is an example of a vulnerability related to:
questions.explanation: An unsupported system.** Using an operating system that is past its end-of-life (EOL) is a major vulnerability because the vendor no longer provides security updates, leaving it exposed to known exploits.

questions.questionText: A system administrator is reviewing server logs and notices that a user account, which should only be active during business hours in a single geographic location, has login attempts from three different continents within a 10-minute window. This is a strong indicator of:
questions.explanation: Impossible travel.** This indicator of compromise occurs when a user account shows activity from geographically distant locations in a time frame that would be impossible for the legitimate user to travel between.

questions.questionText: A user reports that their computer is running extremely slowly and a program they don't recognize is consuming a large amount of CPU and memory. Upon investigation, a security analyst determines the program is capturing keystrokes and sending them to a remote server. What type of malware is this?
questions.explanation: Keylogger.** A keylogger is a type of spyware that records keystrokes to capture sensitive information like usernames, passwords, and credit card numbers.

questions.questionText: To prevent a single point of compromise from affecting the entire network, a security architect recommends dividing the network into smaller, isolated zones based on function (e.g., HR, Finance, Development). Each zone has its own access controls. This mitigation technique is known as:
questions.explanation: Segmentation.** Network segmentation divides a network into smaller, isolated subnets to limit the lateral movement of an attacker and contain breaches.

questions.questionText: A company implements a policy that ensures users only have the permissions necessary to perform their job responsibilities. For example, a marketing employee cannot access financial databases. This is an application of which security principle?
questions.explanation: Least privilege.** The principle of least privilege dictates that users and systems should only be granted the minimum levels of access—or permissions—necessary to perform their duties.

questions.questionText: A disgruntled former employee, who still has an active account, logs into the company's sales database and deletes several critical records out of revenge. This action is carried out by which type of threat actor?
questions.explanation: Insider threat.** An insider threat originates from within the organization and involves a current or former employee, contractor, or partner who has authorized access and misuses it.

questions.questionText: A manufacturing company relies on a third-party vendor to manage its industrial control systems. A security breach at this vendor leads to a compromise of the manufacturing company's network. This is an example of an attack targeting the:
questions.explanation: Supply chain.** A supply chain attack targets a trusted third-party vendor or supplier that has access to an organization's systems or data.

questions.questionText: A web developer is testing a new feature and discovers that by manipulating a URL parameter, they can execute arbitrary database queries, including one that dumps the entire user table. This is a classic example of what type of vulnerability?
questions.explanation: SQL injection (SQLi).** SQLi is a web-based vulnerability that allows an attacker to interfere with the queries that an application makes to its database.

questions.questionText: A security operations center (SOC) analyst receives an alert for an unusually high volume of failed login attempts against a critical server, followed by a successful login. This pattern is a strong indicator of what type of attack?
questions.explanation: Brute force.** A brute-force attack consists of an attacker trying many passwords or passphrases with the hope of eventually guessing correctly. A high volume of failed logins followed by a success is a classic sign.

questions.questionText: An attacker sets up a rogue wireless access point in a coffee shop with the same name as the shop's legitimate Wi-Fi network. When users connect to it, the attacker captures their unencrypted traffic. This is a form of which type of attack?
questions.explanation: Wireless attack.** This scenario describes an "evil twin" attack, a common type of wireless attack where an attacker sets up a malicious access point to intercept traffic.

questions.questionText: A security team is implementing a new endpoint security policy. One of the requirements is to create a list of all approved software and prevent any other applications from being installed or executed. This mitigation technique is known as:
questions.explanation: Application allow list.** An application allow list is a security measure that explicitly defines which applications are authorized to run on a system, blocking all others.

questions.questionText: A group of politically motivated attackers launches a massive DDoS attack against a government website, making it unavailable to the public. Their goal is to protest a new policy. Which of the following best describes this threat actor and their motivation?
questions.optionA: Organized crime motivated by financial gain
questions.explanation: Hacktivist motivated by philosophical/political beliefs.** Hacktivists are individuals or groups who use hacking to promote a political agenda or social change.

questions.questionText: A user finds a USB drive in the company parking lot and, out of curiosity, plugs it into their workstation. The drive automatically executes a malicious payload that installs a backdoor. This attack was delivered via which threat vector?
questions.explanation: Removable device.** Using a found USB drive is a classic example of how removable media can be used as a vector to introduce malware into a secure environment.

questions.questionText: A security researcher discovers a flaw in a widely used encryption algorithm that allows an attacker to decrypt traffic much more easily than expected. This represents what type of vulnerability?
questions.explanation: Cryptographic vulnerability.** A flaw in an encryption algorithm, its implementation, or its key management can create a cryptographic vulnerability that weakens its security.

questions.questionText: A security analyst is investigating a data breach and finds that the attacker was able to move from a compromised web server to a critical database server that was supposed to be on an isolated network segment. This failure to contain the attack highlights a weakness in which mitigation technique?
questions.explanation: Segmentation.** The attacker's ability to move between network segments indicates that the segmentation was not properly implemented or enforced, failing to isolate the critical database server.

questions.questionText: An organization is phasing out an old server that is no longer needed. To mitigate potential vulnerabilities, the IT team securely wipes the data, removes it from the network, and formally documents its retirement. This process is known as:
questions.explanation: Decommissioning.** Decommissioning is the formal process of taking an asset out of service, including data sanitization, and removing network access to prevent it from becoming a future liability.

modules.title: Module 3: Security Architecture
modules.description: Architecture models, securing enterprise infrastructure, data protection, resilience, and recovery strategies.

lectures.title: Day 7: Architecture Models and Infrastructure Concepts
lectures.content:
# Day 7 — Architecture Models and Infrastructure Concepts

## Module 3: Security Architecture | Session 7 of 14

| | |
|:---|:---|
| **Duration** | 2 hours (120 minutes) |
| **Exam Domain** | 3.0 — Security Architecture (18%) |
| **Objectives Covered** | 3.1 |
| **Delivery** | Live online (Zoom/Teams), bilingual English/Arabic |

---

## Session Overview

Module 3 shifts the course from individual threats and controls to the architectural decisions that define an organization's security posture at scale. This session covers the full range of architecture and infrastructure models that appear on the SY0-701 exam — from cloud computing and serverless architectures to industrial control systems and embedded devices. The breadth of this objective is significant: students must understand the security implications of cloud responsibility matrices, infrastructure as code, microservices, containerization, virtualization, IoT, ICS/SCADA, and real-time operating systems.

Beyond the technology models themselves, students will learn the considerations that drive architecture decisions: availability, resilience, cost, responsiveness, scalability, ease of deployment, risk transference, ease of recovery, patch availability, power, and compute. These considerations are not theoretical — they are the trade-offs that security architects evaluate daily when designing or reviewing enterprise infrastructure. The exam tests students' ability to weigh these factors in scenario-based questions.

This session is conceptually broad rather than technically deep. The goal is to ensure students can recognize each architecture model, understand its security implications, and evaluate the trade-offs involved in choosing one model over another.

---

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this session, students will be able to:

1. **Explain** the shared responsibility model for cloud security and identify where responsibility lies for IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS.
2. **Compare** infrastructure concepts: IaC, serverless, microservices, containerization, and virtualization.
3. **Describe** the security implications of IoT, ICS/SCADA, RTOS, and embedded systems.
4. **Differentiate** between physical isolation (air-gapped), logical segmentation, and software-defined networking (SDN).
5. **Evaluate** architecture considerations including availability, resilience, scalability, cost, and risk transference.
6. **Analyze** a scenario to recommend the most appropriate architecture model based on security requirements.

---

## Exam Objectives Covered

| Objective | Description |
|:---|:---|
| **3.1** | Compare and contrast security implications of different architecture models |

---

## Detailed Session Outline

| Time Block | Duration | Topic | Activity Type | Details |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 0:00–0:05 | 5 min | **Module 3 Introduction** | Lecture | Welcome to Module 3. Explain the shift from individual controls to architectural thinking. Preview the three sessions in this module. |
| 0:05–0:25 | 20 min | **Cloud Architecture and Security** | Lecture + Diagram | Cover cloud models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS) and the **Responsibility matrix** (shared responsibility model — who secures what at each layer). **Hybrid considerations** (mixing on-premises and cloud — complexity of managing security across both). **Third-party vendors** (cloud providers as trusted third parties — vendor lock-in, data sovereignty concerns). Use a visual table showing responsibility split for each cloud model. |
| 0:25–0:35 | 10 min | **Infrastructure as Code (IaC) and Serverless** | Lecture | **IaC** — managing infrastructure through code/templates (Terraform, CloudFormation) rather than manual configuration. Security benefit: consistency, version control, auditability. Risk: misconfigured templates can deploy insecure infrastructure at scale. **Serverless** — code runs without managing servers (AWS Lambda, Azure Functions). Security benefit: no OS to patch. Risk: increased reliance on the cloud provider's security, function-level vulnerabilities. |
| 0:35–0:50 | 15 min | **Microservices, Containerization, and Virtualization** | Lecture + Diagram | **Microservices** — application architecture where each function runs as an independent service. Security benefit: isolation of components. Risk: increased attack surface, complex inter-service communication. **Containerization** (Docker, Kubernetes) — lightweight isolation of applications. Security benefit: consistent deployment. Risk: shared kernel, container escape vulnerabilities. **Virtualization** — running multiple OS instances on a single physical host. Security benefit: isolation between VMs. Risk: VM escape, hypervisor vulnerabilities. Compare containers vs. VMs. |
| 0:50–1:05 | 15 min | **Network Infrastructure Models** | Lecture | **Physical isolation / Air-gapped** — completely disconnected from external networks. Used for classified systems, critical infrastructure. Most secure but least flexible. **Logical segmentation** — using VLANs, subnets, and firewall rules to separate traffic on shared infrastructure. **Software-defined networking (SDN)** — programmatic control of network behavior through software. Security benefit: rapid, automated policy enforcement. Risk: centralized controller is a single point of failure. Cover **On-premises** vs. cloud. **Centralized vs. decentralized** architectures. |
| 1:05–1:10 | 5 min | **Break** | — | — |
| 1:10–1:25 | 15 min | **IoT, ICS/SCADA, RTOS, and Embedded Systems** | Lecture | **IoT** — internet-connected devices (cameras, sensors, smart appliances). Security challenges: limited compute for security software, default credentials, infrequent patching. **ICS/SCADA** — industrial control systems managing physical processes (power grids, water treatment, manufacturing). Security challenges: legacy protocols, availability paramount, cannot easily patch. **RTOS** — real-time operating systems for time-critical applications. Security challenges: limited security features, long lifecycles. **Embedded systems** — purpose-built computing systems within larger devices. Security challenges: firmware vulnerabilities, difficult to update. **High availability** — designing systems to minimize downtime. |
| 1:25–1:45 | 20 min | **Architecture Considerations** | Lecture + Discussion | Systematic coverage of all considerations: **Availability** (uptime requirements), **Resilience** (ability to recover from failures), **Cost** (budget constraints driving architecture choices), **Responsiveness** (latency requirements), **Scalability** (ability to grow with demand), **Ease of deployment** (how quickly can new systems be provisioned), **Risk transference** (shifting risk to third parties — cloud providers, insurance), **Ease of recovery** (how quickly can systems be restored after failure), **Patch availability** (can the system be patched? How quickly?), **Inability to patch** (some systems cannot be patched — ICS, embedded — requiring compensating controls), **Power** (power requirements and redundancy), **Compute** (processing capacity requirements). |
| 1:45–2:05 | 20 min | **Architecture Decision Exercise** | Interactive Activity | Present 5 scenarios. Students must recommend an architecture model and justify their choice based on the considerations discussed. Example: "A government agency needs to process classified intelligence data with zero internet connectivity" → Air-gapped, on-premises, high availability. |
| 2:05–2:15 | 10 min | **Session Summary & Preview** | Wrap-up | Recap architecture models and considerations. Preview Day 8: Securing Enterprise Infrastructure. |

---

## Key Concepts & Definitions

| Term | Definition |
|:---|:---|
| **Shared Responsibility Model** | A framework defining which security responsibilities belong to the cloud provider and which belong to the customer, varying by service model (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS). |
| **Infrastructure as Code (IaC)** | Managing and provisioning infrastructure through machine-readable configuration files rather than manual processes. |
| **Serverless** | A cloud computing model where the provider manages the server infrastructure and the customer only deploys code (functions). |
| **Microservices** | An architectural approach where an application is built as a collection of small, independent services that communicate over APIs. |
| **Containerization** | A lightweight virtualization method that packages an application and its dependencies into an isolated container sharing the host OS kernel. |
| **Air-Gapped** | A network or system that is physically isolated from all external networks, including the internet. |
| **SDN (Software-Defined Networking)** | An approach to networking where the control plane is separated from the data plane and managed through software, enabling programmatic network configuration. |
| **ICS/SCADA** | Industrial Control Systems / Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition — systems that monitor and control industrial processes such as power generation, water treatment, and manufacturing. |
| **RTOS (Real-Time Operating System)** | An operating system designed to process data and events within strict time constraints, used in time-critical applications. |
| **Embedded System** | A computer system with a dedicated function within a larger mechanical or electronic system, often with limited resources. |
| **Risk Transference** | A risk management strategy where risk is shifted to a third party, such as a cloud provider or insurance company. |
| **High Availability** | A system design approach that ensures a high level of operational continuity and minimal downtime. |

---

## Real-World Examples & Scenarios

**Scenario 1 — Cloud Responsibility Matrix in Practice**
A fintech startup in Amman uses AWS (IaaS) to host its banking application. The startup is responsible for securing the operating system, application code, data encryption, and access management. AWS is responsible for the physical data center, hypervisor, and network infrastructure. When a data breach occurs due to a misconfigured S3 bucket (publicly accessible), the startup — not AWS — is liable, because data configuration is the customer's responsibility under the shared responsibility model.

**Scenario 2 — ICS/SCADA Security in the Energy Sector**
A power utility in Saudi Arabia operates SCADA systems that control electrical grid distribution. These systems run on legacy protocols (Modbus, DNP3) that were designed for reliability, not security — they lack authentication and encryption. The systems cannot be easily patched because downtime could cause power outages. The utility implements compensating controls: network segmentation (isolating SCADA from the corporate network), monitoring (anomaly detection on SCADA traffic), and physical security (restricting access to control rooms).

**Scenario 3 — Containerization Security**
A technology company in Dubai deploys its microservices application using Docker containers orchestrated by Kubernetes. A vulnerability in one container allows an attacker to escape the container and access the host OS kernel (container escape). Because containers share the host kernel — unlike VMs, which have their own OS — a container escape can compromise all containers on the same host. The company mitigates this by implementing container image scanning, running containers with least privilege, and using network policies to restrict inter-container communication.

---

## Instructor Notes

**Common Misconceptions:**
- Students often confuse **containers** and **virtual machines**. Key difference: VMs include a full OS and run on a hypervisor; containers share the host OS kernel and are lighter weight. VMs provide stronger isolation; containers provide faster deployment.
- **Serverless** does not mean "no servers." Servers exist — the cloud provider manages them. The customer only manages the code.
- Students may think **air-gapped** systems are invulnerable. They are not — Stuxnet demonstrated that air-gapped systems can be compromised through removable media (USB drives).
- **Risk transference** does not eliminate risk. It shifts the financial or operational burden to a third party, but the organization retains reputational risk and must still manage the relationship.

**Exam Emphasis:**
- The shared responsibility model is heavily tested. Students must know what the customer vs. the provider is responsible for at each service level (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS).
- IoT and ICS/SCADA questions focus on the unique security challenges: inability to patch, default credentials, legacy protocols, and the priority of availability over confidentiality.
- Architecture consideration questions present trade-offs: "Which consideration is MOST important when designing a system for a hospital's patient monitoring?" → Availability.

**Teaching Tips:**
- For the shared responsibility model, draw a layered diagram (physical → network → OS → application → data) and show where the responsibility line falls for IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS.
- For containers vs. VMs, use the analogy: VMs are like separate houses (each with its own foundation); containers are like apartments in a building (shared foundation/structure).
- For ICS/SCADA, show real images of industrial control systems to make the concept tangible for students who work primarily in IT.

---

## Discussion Questions

1. "Your company is migrating from on-premises servers to a cloud IaaS provider. What security responsibilities transfer to the provider, and what remains yours?"

2. "A hospital's patient monitoring system runs on an embedded RTOS that cannot be patched. The vendor is out of business. What compensating controls would you implement?"

3. "Your organization uses microservices with 50 independent services communicating over APIs. How does this architecture increase the attack surface compared to a monolithic application?"

4. "An air-gapped military network is considered the most secure architecture. What are its limitations, and how could it still be compromised?"

---

## Hands-On Activity: Architecture Model Selection

**Objective:** Students evaluate 5 organizational requirements and recommend the most appropriate architecture model, justifying their choice based on the considerations covered in this session.

| # | Requirement | Recommended Architecture | Key Considerations |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 1 | A classified government intelligence processing system with zero internet connectivity. | Air-gapped, on-premises, physically isolated | Availability, resilience, inability to patch (compensating controls needed) |
| 2 | A startup building a mobile app that needs to scale rapidly during peak usage and minimize infrastructure management. | Cloud (PaaS or serverless), containerized microservices | Scalability, cost, ease of deployment, responsiveness |
| 3 | A manufacturing plant with legacy control systems managing assembly line robots. | ICS/SCADA with network segmentation, compensating controls | Availability (paramount), inability to patch, power, resilience |
| 4 | A regional bank that must comply with data sovereignty regulations requiring customer data to remain within Jordan. | Hybrid cloud (on-premises for regulated data, cloud for non-sensitive workloads) | Cost, data sovereignty, risk transference, ease of recovery |
| 5 | A research university deploying hundreds of IoT sensors across campus for environmental monitoring. | IoT architecture with dedicated network segment, centralized management | Scalability, patch availability, default credential management, monitoring |

---

## Session Summary

- **Cloud architectures** operate under a shared responsibility model — the customer's security responsibilities vary by service model (IaaS > PaaS > SaaS).
- **IaC** provides consistency and auditability but can propagate misconfigurations at scale.
- **Serverless** and **containerization** reduce operational overhead but introduce new attack surfaces (function vulnerabilities, container escape).
- **Network infrastructure** ranges from air-gapped (most isolated) to SDN (most programmable), with logical segmentation as the common middle ground.
- **IoT, ICS/SCADA, RTOS, and embedded systems** share common challenges: limited compute, inability to patch, default credentials, and long lifecycles.
- Architecture decisions are driven by **considerations**: availability, resilience, cost, scalability, risk transference, patch availability, and more.
- On the exam, expect questions requiring you to match architecture models to requirements and evaluate trade-offs between considerations.

---

## Preparation for Next Session

Day 8 covers **securing enterprise infrastructure** (objective 3.2) — the practical application of security principles to network devices, firewalls, VPNs, and communication protocols. Students will learn about device placement, security zones, failure modes, network appliances (jump servers, proxy servers, IPS/IDS, load balancers), port security (802.1X, EAP), firewall types (WAF, UTM, NGFW), and secure communication technologies (VPN, TLS, IPSec, SD-WAN, SASE). This is one of the most network-focused sessions in the course.
